notes.meaning: Jesus chose seventy (or seventy-two) followers and sent them out in pairs ahead of Him. They were to visit every town He planned to go to and prepare the people for His coming. Traveling two by two gave them companions for encouragement and provided two witnesses to confirm their message.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern scholars question whether this mission took place, seeing it as a doublet of the sending of the twelve apostles because the instructions are so similar.

notes.meaning: Jesus told them that many people were ready to hear the good news, like a field full of ripe grain ready for harvest. The problem was that there were very few faithful workers to gather them in. He urged them to pray that God, the true owner of the harvest, would send out more workers into the world.

Jesus sent His followers out with a warning that they would be like gentle lambs surrounded by vicious wolves. They would face opposition and danger from people who hated their message. Even so, they could go out boldly because the Lord who sent them would watch over them.

The travelers were told to pack light, taking no money bag, traveler's pouch, or extra sandals. They were also told not to stop and greet people along the road. Eastern greetings were long and formal ceremonies, and the disciples had an urgent message that could not afford wasted time.

Whenever the disciples arrived at a house, their first words were to offer a blessing of peace. This was more than a polite greeting; it was an offer of God's favor and goodwill. It set a gentle tone and opened the door to share the gospel.

If the person living there welcomed their peaceful message, God's peace would stay and rest upon that home. If the household turned them away, that blessing would not be wasted but would return to the disciples. God does not force His gifts on the unwilling, but His messengers keep their own peace.

The disciples were told to stay in the first house that welcomed them rather than moving around to find better food or lodging. They could gladly eat and drink whatever was offered, because workers deserve to receive their living. Taking care of their daily needs was fair pay for their spiritual service, not charity.

When an entire town welcomed them, the messengers were to eat whatever food was placed in front of them without complaining. They were not to worry about strict religious food customs or burden their hosts with special demands. Staying focused on their preaching mattered far more than what was on the table.

Jesus told them to heal the sick in that town as proof of God's power and kindness. Then they were to proclaim that the kingdom of God had arrived near them. These miracles showed that God's royal rule was already breaking into the world through Jesus.

differ.view: Some hold that the kingdom of God spoken of here is entirely in the future and did not begin during Jesus' earthly ministry.

notes.meaning: If a town refused to welcome them, the disciples were to go out into the public streets and deliver a final warning. By wiping off the town's dust from their feet, they showed they were free of blame for what happened next. Even then, they still reminded the people that God's kingdom had come near them.

Jesus warned that on the final day of judgment, it will be easier for the ancient city of Sodom than for a town that rejected His messengers. Sodom was famous for wickedness, but its people never heard the good news of Christ. Rejecting the direct offer of God's grace brings a far heavier guilt.

Jesus spoke words of deep sorrow and warning over the towns of Chorazin and Bethsaida because they did not turn from sin after seeing His miracles. Even notoriously wicked Gentile cities like Tyre and Sidon would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes if they had witnessed such signs. For that reason, those ancient cities will face a lighter judgment than places that saw Jesus and ignored Him.

Capernaum had enjoyed the highest privilege because Jesus lived and taught there so often. Instead of being lifted up to heaven for its pride, it would be brought down to the depths of ruin. Great spiritual advantages will only lead to greater grief if we refuse to believe.

Jesus gave His workers the authority of official ambassadors. Anyone who listened to them was listening to Jesus, and anyone who despised them was despising Christ and the Father who sent Him. A person's reaction to faithful teaching reveals how they truly treat God.

The disciples returned full of excitement because even evil spirits obeyed them when they commanded them in Jesus' name. They had only been told to heal the sick, so this victory over demons was a wonderful surprise. They gave Jesus all the credit, knowing the power came entirely from His name.

Jesus answered that He saw Satan falling from heaven as fast as a flash of lightning. While the disciples were casting out demons, Jesus saw the devil's rule over human hearts being shattered. The gospel's advance marks the sudden and sure downfall of the enemy's kingdom.

Jesus granted His followers power over all the spiritual forces of the enemy, describing evil spirits as snakes and scorpions. He promised that nothing Satan tried would truly harm their souls or stop their work. Believers are given divine protection and victory as they carry out the Lord's mission.

Jesus urged them not to make miracles and power over demons their greatest reason for joy. Instead, their true joy should be that their names are permanently enrolled in heaven as God's children. Having eternal life and belonging to God's family is far better than any spiritual gift or earthly success.

In that moment Jesus rejoiced through the Holy Spirit and gave praise to the Father, the Lord of all creation. He praised God for hiding the truth of the gospel from the proud and self-important, while opening it up to simple, humble people like little children. God chose this way because it pleased Him and puts human pride to shame.

differ.view: God's hiding and revealing of truth comes from His sovereign, eternal choice to save whom He pleases without any merit of their own.
God does not hide truth on a whim, but shields it from those who proudly rely on their own wisdom while warmly revealing it to the humble.
